A pull request changes every async method in an API's data layer from

, with the description "ValueTask is the allocation-free Task." The load test after the merge shows the same allocation rate and the same latency as before. Nearly every one of those methods queries the database, so each call completes asynchronously and allocates just as it did. Meanwhile, the change quietly broke a rule in a helper that awaits the same lookup twice, once for the total and once for the log line. It passes every test today, and the docs say its behavior is undefined.

There's real substance behind it. The .NET team introduced

precisely to cut allocations, and hot APIs in the base libraries, such as stream and socket reads, return it. Benchmarks of those APIs show real savings. And the name, with "Value" on the front, sounds like the
What the name hides is that the saving depends on how the method completes, and that the struct comes with rules its callers must follow.
Where a Task's cost comes from
When an async method has to wait, something on the heap must represent the operation in flight: the caller holds it, and the code after the

stored in a variable or field as a bug until proven otherwise.
The textbook case is a hot method that usually has its answer ready, like a cache in front of a slower store. A hit returns the value inside the struct; only a miss pays for a
